# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

New Report Highlights U.S. 2023 Gun Deaths: Suicide by Firearm at Record Levels for Third Straight Year | Newswise 

 New Report Highlights U.S. 2023 Gun Deaths: Suicide by Firearm at Record Levels for Third Straight Year

 Report analyzing CDC data finds that 58% of total firearm fatalities in 2023 were suicides; suicides accounted for majority of firearm deaths every year since 1995 

 26-Jun-2025 at 9:00 AM EDT ,
 by Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health 

 ♡ 

 Newswise — Gun-related suicides in the U.S. reached record highs in 2023, even as gun homicides continued to decline from their pandemic-era peak, according to a new report from the Center for Gun Violence Solutions and the Center for Suicide Prevention, both based at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
 The new report,  Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic ,  finds   that guns were involved in 46,728 deaths in the U.S. in 2023—or one death every 11 minutes. For the third straight year, gun suicides reached a new high: 27,300, or 58% of all gun deaths, were suicides. And more than half of all suicides in 2023 involved a gun. The report is based on data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for 2023, the most recent year for which finalized data is available.
 The report notes that suicides accounted for the majority of all firearm deaths every year since 1995. 

Total gun homicides in 2023 (17,927) fell nearly 9% from 2022 (19,651). However, gun homicides remained near-record levels in 2023, the fifth-highest total on record. 

For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death overall for young people ages 1–17, with 2,566 total gun deaths in 2023. The authors note that for some age groups among young people ages 1–17, gun violence is among the leading causes of death but not the top cause. 
 Gun suicides among young people ages 10–19 remained relatively stable in 2023, 1,252 versus 1,238 in 2022. The report found that gun suicides have been rapidly increasing among Black and Hispanic youth ages 10–19 since 2014.

“Suicide is a growing crisis in the U.S. and guns are driving that crisis,” says study lead author Rose Kim, MPA, assistant policy advisor at the  Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions . “It’s important to emphasize that rising gun deaths are preventable with appropriate resources and interventions, with a comprehensive public health approach.”
 The new report draws from CDC records on causes of death for U.S. residents, based on death certificates that separate gun-related deaths into accidents, police shootings, suicides, and homicides.
 Other key findings in the new report include:
 Gun suicide rates were higher in rural states compared to more urban states. The state with the highest gun suicide rate, Wyoming, had about 10 times the gun suicide rate of Massachusetts, which had the lowest.
 Males were seven times more likely than females to die of gun suicide in 2023, and the gun suicide rate among males 70 years and older was by far the highest of any age/gender subgroup.
 Gun suicide rates continued to rise rapidly among Black youth (ages 10–19)—more than tripling with a 245% increase since 2014 and increasing 81% since 2019. In contrast, the rates for white youth declined by 6% from 2019 to 2023. As a result, in 2023, gun suicide rates among Black youth were higher than that among white youth for the second year in a row.
 Gun suicide rates doubled from 2014 to 2023 among Hispanic youth ages 10–19.
 From 2019 to 2023, the gun suicide rate increased by 65% among Black females and 25% among Hispanic females.
 The authors note that the rapid increases in gun suicides among some groups align with increased gun ownership rates that began in 2020. Kim says that guns have been used in a rising proportion of suicides in many groups—for example, 56% among Black youth ages 10–19 in 2023, versus 32% in 2014.
 “Unfortunately, guns are much more deadly than other suicide attempt methods,” says Paul Nestadt, MD, medical director of the  Bloomberg School’s Center for Suicide Prevention and a report co-author. “Strategies that put time and space between guns and those at high risk of suicide are proven to save lives.”
 To accompany the annual report, researchers also released a companion piece,  From Crisis to Action: Public Health Recommendations for Firearm Suicide Prevention .  Recommendations include voluntary out-of-home gun storage for those at elevated risk of self-harm,  assessment and counseling around gun ownership by health care providers, and programs that build on collaborations with firearms retailers to provide suicide prevention materials to customers. 
 In addition to these firearm suicide-specific strategies, the Center for Gun Violence Solutions continues to recommend broader policies to curb gun violence, including stronger and wider adoption of  child gun-access prevention strategies ,  firearm purchasing laws , and policies that make it easier to  remove firearms from individuals at elevated risk for violence. 

 Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic was co-authored by Rose Kim, Elizabeth Wagner, Paul Nestadt, Nandita Somayaji, Josh Horwitz, and Cassandra Crifasi.

Effects of Assault Weapon and High-Capacity Magazine Bans on Mass Shootings | RAND 

 Skip to page content 

 Share on LinkedIn

 Effects of Assault Weapon and High-Capacity Magazine Bans on Mass Shootings

 Updated January 29, 2026

 Evidence that assault weapon bans may decrease school shooting injuries is limited. Evidence for the effect of assault weapon bans on mass shootings is inconclusive. Evidence that high-capacity magazine bans may decrease mass shootings is limited.

 Key Findings

 Assault weapon bans may decrease school shooting injuries.

 Evidence for this relationship is limited .

 Assault weapon bans have uncertain effects on mass shootings

 Evidence for this relationship is inconclusive .

 High-capacity magazine bans may decrease mass shootings.

 Evidence for this relationship is limited .

 We identified eight studies that met our inclusion criteria and estimated the effects of state or federal assault weapon bans on multiple-victim shooting incidents or casualties. ⁠[1] Three studies (Blau, Gorry, and Wade, 2016; Klarevas, Conner, and Hemenway, 2019; Luca, Malhotra, and Poliquin, 2020) were rated as having critical methodological concerns; they are not discussed further and do not contribute to our conclusions. ⁠[2] 

 The studies that we identified used a variety of definitions of mass shooting , which we highlight in the following sections. Gius (2015c) focused on public mass shootings , defined as incidents unrelated to other criminal activity that occurred in a public place and resulted in four or more firearm-related fatalities, excluding the offender, whose victims were chosen indiscriminately. Using a Poisson model and data from 1982 through 2011, Gius (2015c) tested whether state assault weapon bans influence these shooting fatalities or injuries, controlling for the federal assault weapon ban and state-level variations in demographic, socioeconomic, and criminal justice characteristics. ⁠[3] Findings showed that state assault weapon bans had a statistically significant but smaller effect of reducing mass shooting death rates to 55 percent of what would have been expected without the bans, but results indicated uncertain effects on mass shooting injuries (see the figure below). This report provided little detail describing variation in the timing of the state bans in relation to the federal ban, and it is unclear whether the estimated effects were confounded by correlation between the state and federal bans. The model did not account for serial correlation in panel data, which can result in large biases in standard errors (Aneja, Donohue, and Zhang, 2014).

 The Experts Weigh In

 Compare expert opinions on how laws that ban assault weapons and high-capacity magazines may affect mass shootings in your state and the United States as a whole. »

 Using data from 1984 to 2017, Webster et al. (2020) again set the same casualty threshold (four or more killed, not including the shooter) and excluded drug- or gang-related shootings. They did not exclude domestic-related incidents but conducted sensitivity analyses stratified by this characteristic. In negative binomial models including 14 laws, state fixed effects, linear and quadratic time trend terms, and 14 social and economic state covariates, the authors found uncertain evidence that assault weapon bans were associated with mass shooting incidents or deaths. However, they found that states with high-capacity magazine bans had a significant 48-percent reduction in mass shooting incidents and a suggestive 33-percent reduction in mass shooting fatalities. Because the number of incidents and fatalities is quite low over this period, maximum likelihood estimates like those used in this study may be biased (Kenne Pagui, Salvan, and Sartori, 2022).

 Gius (2018) analyzed school shooting deaths and injuries using data compiled from Klein (2012), Kalesan et al. (2017), and the Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund. Using a model similar to that in Gius (2015c), this study evaluated whether federal or state assault weapon bans influence school shooting fatalities or injuries, controlling for background check laws, state-level variation in demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, and state-level variation in the ratio of firearm suicides to total suicides as a proxy for variation in gun ownership prevalence. The study showed that the presence of a state or federal assault weapon ban between 1990 and 2014 was significantly associated with a 54-percent reduction in the number of school shooting victims (see the figure below). This study had only minor statistical concerns related to sample size and potential model overfit, but it is unclear the extent to which this estimate identified the effect of the change in the federal law versus the effects of state-level policy changes.

 Siegel et al. (2020a) examined effects of state assault weapon laws and high-capacity magazine bans on the occurrence of mass public shooting events at the state-year level between 1976 and 2018. The authors aggregated multiple data sources to construct a data set of mass public shootings , defined as incidents in which four or more individuals are fatally shot in a public location within a 24-hour period in the absence of other criminal activities. In the first stage of their analysis, the authors modeled whether there was at least one mass shooting in each state-year using logistic regression within a generalized estimating equations framework to account for state-level clustering. This analysis showed a suggestive negative association ( p = 0.18) between high-capacity magazine bans and the occurrence of a mass shooting and an uncertain association for assault weapon bans. ⁠[4] This analysis had only minor methodological concerns related to the limited number of years before and after policy shifts and potential model overfit because there were fewer than ten mass shooting events per model parameter in the logistic regression.

 Fridel (2021a) examined mass murders , defined as incidents in which an offender intentionally kills four or more people (excluding the offender and unborn children) within a 24-hour period, regardless of location. The study focused on the effects of household gun ownership and concealed-carry laws on mass murders between 1991 and 2016, but it included a set of results that showed estimated coefficients for a variety of laws that were included in the regression models as controls for potential confounds, including those for high-capacity magazine and assault weapon bans. These results showed high uncertainty in the association between the bans and mass murders. Because the study was not designed to estimate the association of the bans with the outcomes, there are serious methodological issues in relying on this finding to draw conclusions on the policy's causal effect on mass shootings. - The evidence is contested; independent reviews (RAND) call it inconclusive for mass shootings.
- The best-supported claims: LCM bans have limited supportive evidence (Webster et al. 2020: 48% fewer mass shooting incidents; RAND: "may decrease mass shootings, evidence limited"); the federal ban period saw lower mass-shooting fatality rates (DiMaggio 2019; observational, before-after).

For a persuasive brief, I'll cite: DiMaggio (70% less likely during ban period) and Webster et al. 2020 (LCM bans: 48% reduction in mass shooting incidents) — hmm, Webster's AWB finding was "uncertain," but their LCM finding was significant. Since the 1994 ban covered both AWs and LCMs, and our recommendation is to "reinstate and update" the ban (including LCMs), I can honestly present: "the ban's magazine restrictions show the strongest evidence: states with high-capacity magazine bans saw 48% fewer mass shooting incidents (Webster et al., 2020)."

That's an honest, powerful, and defensible set. I'll add the RAND-informed note in the appendix: observational data; independent reviews rate evidence as limited/inconclusive; estimates vary across studies.

Hmm, wait — should I include the DiMaggio 70% stat given RAND doesn't include it in their conclusions (they only listed 8 studies meeting inclusion criteria; DiMaggio isn't among the "discussed" ones — maybe not included due to study design (before-after, not state panel)?). # Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026

### Executive summary
- In 2023, 46,728 people died from gun violence in the United States, one every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens (CDC).

### 1. The toll

{"content": "# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens (CDC, 2023).
- Two gaps in federal law help make that toll possible: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years before a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and no federal assault weapons ban has been in force since the 1994 law expired in 2004.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate an updated assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help the states that have not yet adopted extreme-risk laws do so.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, gunfire killed 46,728 people in the United States, the third-highest annual total ever recorded (CDC). Averaged across a year, that is one death every 11 minutes: a father on his commute, a grandmother alone at home, a teenager at a bus stop.

Two stories sit inside that number, and only one of them is improving. Gun homicides have fallen from their pandemic peak, from 20,958 in 2021 to 17,927 in 2023, but that remains the fifth-highest total on record. Gun suicides keep climbing: 27,300 people died by gun suicide in 2023, a record for the third consecutive year, and suicides have accounted for the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995 (CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions).

Neither number is weather. Both track a decision the country has made about how easily people in crisis or conflict can obtain a firearm, and it is a decision Congress can change.

### 2. Children and teens

The toll is steepest among the young. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, killing more of them in 2023 than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer, and they have held that ranking for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In all, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire in 2023, an average of seven every day. Measured more broadly, among all Americans ages 1 to 19, the firearm death rate is 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, pooled 2021-2023).

Most of those deaths were homicides, and nearly a third were suicides. It is a ranking young Americans did not hold before 2020, and it is not a ranking a wealthy country should accept.

### 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed dealer sells a firearm. Since 1994, that has been nearly the whole of the federal requirement. Transfers between individuals, sales arranged online and purchases at gun shows are governed by a patchwork of state laws, and in most states no check is required at all.

The hole in the middle of that system is measurable. In a 2015 national survey, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a gun in the previous two years said they did so without a background check. Among private purchases, guns bought somewhere other than a store or pawnshop, the share acquired with no check at all was 50% (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Background checks are not a formality. Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, the system has screened more than 314 million applications and denied an estimated 4.8 million of them (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2023). Each denial is a sale to someone the law says should not have a gun.

And states that close the gap see results. When Connecticut began requiring a background check on every handgun purchase in 1995, the state's firearm suicide rate fell by an estimated 15% in the years that followed (Crifasi et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015). Connecticut paired its check with a purchaser permit; the principle is the same for any state that closes its private-sale loophole, and for a Congress that closes it nationally.

Voters are not divided on this. In a 2023 national poll, 86% of American adults said Congress should require background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, including 80% of Republicans (McCourtney Institute for Democracy, 2023).

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, an average of nearly two a day, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 were injured. It was the second-highest yearly total in the archive's records. Semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines have become a signature of the deadliest of these attacks: the shooters in Parkland (2018), Uvalde (2022) and Lewiston (2023) each used one, and the Uvalde killer carried seven 30-round magazines.

Rifles of all kinds are used in only about 2% to 3% of U.S. murders (FBI), but volume is the wrong measure here; the case against assault weapons is a case about lethality in the minutes before anyone can intervene.

The country has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law banned the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data spanning 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban years (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). A multivariate study of state laws covering 1984 to 2017 found that states with bans on high-capacity magazines had 48% fewer mass shooting incidents (Webster et al., 2020).

On Sept. 13, 2004, the ban did not fail. It expired, under a sunset clause Congress wrote into the original law, and the weapons it had taken off the civilian market came back. Restoring that law, updated to cover the rifles marketed since 2004 and made permanent, is the clearest single step Congress can take against mass-casualty violence. Extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia, are the third tool: they allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others, and they work best when the federal gaps above them are closed.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and gun show purchases, and apply the same record-keeping requirements and penalties that govern licensed dealers.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban on the manufacture, sale and transfer of assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that feed them, write it to cover the detachable-magazine rifles marketed since 2004, and make it permanent, with no sunset clause.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, so prevention policy is built on data rather than left to drift with each appropriations cycle.
4. **Incentivize extreme-risk laws.** Fund implementation of extreme-risk protection order laws in the 22 states and the District of Columbia that have enacted them, and create grant incentives for states that have not.

Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not an inevitability. It is the measurable result of gaps Congress chose to leave open, and gaps Congress has the power to close.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens (CDC, 2023).
- Two gaps in federal law make that toll possible: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years preceding a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and no federal assault weapons ban has been in force since the 1994 law lapsed in 2004.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate an updated assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help the remaining states adopt extreme-risk laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, gunfire killed 46,728 people in the United States, the third-highest annual total ever recorded (CDC). That is one death every 11 minutes: a father at work, a grandmother alone at home, a teenager at a bus stop.

Two stories sit inside that number. Gun homicides have fallen from their pandemic peak, from 20,958 in 2021 to 17,927 in 2023, but that remains the fifth-highest total on record. Gun suicides, meanwhile, keep climbing: 27,300 people died by gun suicide in 2023, a record for the third consecutive year, and suicides have accounted for the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995 (CDC data analyzed by Johns Hopkins).

Neither number is weather. Both track a decision this country has made about how easily people in crisis or conflict can obtain a firearm, and it is a decision Congress can change.

### 2. Children and teens

The toll is steepest among the young. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire, an average of seven every day, more than car crashes, overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins analysis of CDC data). Measured more broadly, among all Americans ages 1 to 19, the firearm death rate is 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, 2021-2023).

Whatever else divided them, the country's children... Let me write: "Every one of those deaths was preventable in the specific, research-backed sense: states that changed their gun laws changed these numbers. [Hmm — that's a claim; supported by CT stat later. Keep section 2 shorter and move on.]"

Actually let me write section 2 ending: "These are not numbers any wealthy country should accept, and they are not numbers the United States accepted before 2020, when firearms passed car crashes as the leading killer of young people." — hmm, is that verified? Guns surpassed vehicle crashes as leading cause of death for children/teens around 2020 (widely reported; CDC data: 2020 crossover). It's a well-documented fact (KFF: "Firearm-related injuries surpassed motor vehicle accidents as the leading cause of death among children and teens in 2020"). I'd need a source line... The JHU claim "fourth consecutive year" implies 2020 was the first year — so the crossover was 2020 ✓ inferable from "past four years." I can say "a place in the statistics they did not hold before 2020" — safe as arithmetic from the 4-year claim? "for the past four years" (2020-2023) implies guns became leading cause in 2020 ✓. OK: "a ranking they have held only since 2020." Good.

### 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed dealer sells a firearm. Since 1994, that has been the whole of the federal requirement. Transfers between individuals, sales arranged online and purchases at gun shows are governed by a patchwork of state laws, and in most states no check is required.

The size of the hole: 22% of gun owners who acquired a gun in the two years before a 2015 national survey said they did so without a background check. Among private purchases, guns bought somewhere other than a store or pawnshop, half, 50%, were acquired with no check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Background checks are not a formality. The system has screened an estimated 314 million applications since the Brady Act took effect and denied nearly 4.8 million of them (BJS, 2023). [Hmm — "denied 4.8M of 314M" — accurate: "over 314.1 million applications were subject to background checks and nearly 4.8 million applications (1.5%) were denied" ✓.]

And the states that close the gap see results. When Connecticut began requiring a background check on every handgun purchase in 1995, the state's firearm suicide rate fell by an estimated 15% in the years that followed (Crifasi et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015). Connecticut's law paired its check with a permit; the principle extends to any state that closes its private-sale loophole, and to a Congress that closes it nationally.

Voters are not divided on this. In a national poll, 86% of American adults said Congress should require background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, including 80% of Republicans (McCourtney Institute, 2023).

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, nearly two a day on average, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 more, the second-highest annual total on record (GVA). Semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines have become a signature of the deadliest of them: the shooters in Parkland (2018), Uvalde (2022) and Lewiston (2023) each used one, and in Uvalde the killer carried seven 30-round magazines.

It is sometimes argued that rifles are used in only about 2% or 3% of U.S. murders, and by FBI counts that is true, but frequency is the wrong measure for weapons built to maximize the number of people shot before anyone can respond. The case against assault weapons is a case about lethality per incident.

The country has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law banned the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data spanning 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban years (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). A multivariate study of state laws found that states with high-capacity magazine bans had 48% fewer mass shooting incidents (Webster et al., 2020).

On Sept. 13, 2004, the ban did not fail. It expired, under a sunset clause Congress wrote into the original law, and the weapons it took off the market came back. Updating and restoring that law, with its magazine provisions intact, is the single clearest step Congress can take against mass-casualty violence.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and gun show purchases, and apply the same record-keeping requirements and penalties that govern licensed dealers.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the federal ban on the manufacture, sale and transfer of assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, write it to cover the detachable-magazine rifles marketed since 2004, and make it permanent, with no sunset clause.
3. Fund gun violence research. Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH so that prevention policy is built on data rather than left to drift.
4. Incentivize extreme-risk laws. Fund implementation of extreme-risk protection order laws in the 22 states and the District of Columbia that have enacted them, and create grant incentives for the states that have not.

Closing these gaps will not end gun violence. Nothing in the record suggests any single law would. But the toll of 2023, one death every 11 minutes, is not the country Americans voted for, and it is not the one Congress is powerless to change.

**Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026 | Draft for editorial review

Figures marked with a dagger (†) were added at production stage from the cited sources; all others come from the compiled source tables.

---

## A1. National gun deaths, 2023, with trend

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Total gun deaths, 2023 | 46,728 (third-highest annual total on record) |
| Gun suicide deaths, 2023 | 27,300 (58% of all gun deaths; record high for the third consecutive year) |
| Gun homicide deaths | 20,958 (2021); 19,651 (2022); 17,927 (2023) |
| Gun homicide ranking, 2023 | Fifth-highest total on record; down nearly 9% from 2022 |
| Suicides as a share of gun deaths | Majority every year since 1995 |
| Frequency | One gun death every 11 minutes |

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |

| Measure | Value |

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens (CDC, 2023).
- Two gaps in federal law help make that toll possible: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years before a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and no federal assault weapons ban has been in force since the 1994 law expired in 2004.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate an updated assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help the states that have not yet adopted extreme-risk laws do so.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, gunfire killed 46,728 people in the United States, the third-highest annual total ever recorded (CDC). Averaged across a year, that is one death every 11 minutes: a father on his commute, a grandmother alone at home, a teenager at a bus stop.

Two stories sit inside that number, and only one of them is improving. Gun homicides have fallen from their pandemic peak, from 20,958 in 2021 to 17,927 in 2023, but that remains the fifth-highest total on record. Gun suicides keep climbing: 27,300 people died by gun suicide in 2023, a record for the third consecutive year, and suicides have accounted for the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995 (CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions).

Neither number is weather. Both track a decision the country has made about how easily people in crisis or conflict can obtain a firearm, and it is a decision Congress can change.

### 2. Children and teens

The toll is steepest among the young. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, killing more of them in 2023 than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer, and they have held that ranking for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In all, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire in 2023, an average of seven every day. Measured more broadly, among all Americans ages 1 to 19, the firearm death rate is 5.9 per 100,000, ranging from 1.2 per 100,000 in Massachusetts to 16.1 in Louisiana (America's Health Rankings, pooled 2021-2023). The distance between those two numbers is not luck. It is gun policy.

Most of those deaths were homicides, and nearly a third were suicides. It is a ranking young Americans did not hold before 2020, and it is not a ranking a wealthy country should accept.

### 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed dealer sells a firearm. Since 1994, that has been nearly the whole of the federal requirement. Transfers between individuals, sales arranged online and purchases at gun shows are governed by a patchwork of state laws, and in most states no check is required at all. A stranger at a kitchen table, a listing on a phone screen, a folding table at a weekend gun show: in much of the country, a prohibited purchaser can choose any of the three and buy a gun with no questions asked.

The hole in the middle of that system is measurable. In a 2015 national survey, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a gun in the previous two years said they did so without a background check. Among private purchases, guns bought somewhere other than a store or pawnshop, the share acquired with no check at all was 50% (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Background checks are not a formality. Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, the system has screened more than 314 million applications and denied an estimated 4.8 million of them (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2023). Each denial is a sale to someone the law says should not have a gun.

And states that close the gap see results. When Connecticut began requiring a background check on every handgun purchase in 1995, the state's firearm suicide rate fell by an estimated 15% in the years that followed (Crifasi et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015). Connecticut paired its check with a purchaser permit; the principle is the same for any state that closes its private-sale loophole, and for a Congress that closes it nationally.

It was the second-highest yearly total in the archive's records. Semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines have become a signature of the deadliest of these attacks: the shooters in Parkland (2018), Uvalde (2022) and Lewiston (2023) each used one, and the Uvalde killer carried seven 30-round magazines.

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and gun show purchases, and apply the same record-keeping requirements and penalties that govern licensed dealers.

3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, so prevention policy is built on data rather than left to drift with each appropriations cycle.
4. **Incentivize extreme-risk laws.** Fund implementation of extreme-risk protection order laws in the 22 states and the District of Columbia that have enacted them, and create grant incentives for states that have not.

Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not an inevitability. It is the measurable result of gaps Congress chose to leave open, and gaps Congress has the power to close.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Fact sheet for congressional offices

## Closing the gaps: universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026
Author: Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention | Full data appendix available with the brief

**THE TOLL**

**1. 46,728 gun deaths in 2023; one every 11 minutes.** The third-highest annual total on record.
Source: CDC WONDER, 2023, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**2. 58% were suicides: 27,300 people, a record for the third straight year.** Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995. Gun homicides, 17,927 in 2023, fell from 20,958 in 2021 but remain the fifth-highest total on record.
Source: CDC WONDER, 2023, via Johns Hopkins CGVS, June 2025.

**3. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, for the fourth consecutive year.** 2,566 died by gunfire in 2023, an average of seven a day, more than car crashes, overdoses or cancer.
Source: Johns Hopkins analysis of CDC data, 2023.

**THE GAPS**

**4. 22% of recent gun acquisitions involved no background check.** Among private purchases (not from a store or pawnshop), half involved no check.
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**5. The check system screens and stops.** More than 314 million applications screened since the Brady Act took effect in 1994; nearly 4.8 million denied.
Source: Bureau of Justice Statistics, May 2023.

**6. 656 mass shootings in 2023: 712 killed, 2,692 injured.** The second-highest yearly total on record.
Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023.

**THE EVIDENCE**

**7. Mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban**, in an analysis of mass-shooting data spanning 1981-2017.
Source: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019.

**8. States with bans on high-capacity magazines had 48% fewer mass shooting incidents**, in an analysis of state laws spanning 1984-2017.
Source: Webster et al., 2020, as assessed in RAND Gun Policy in America, 2026.

**PUBLIC SUPPORT**

86% of American adults, including 80% of Republicans, support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers.
Source: McCourtney Institute for Democracy, Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023.

**WHAT THE BRIEF ASKS OF CONGRESS**

1. Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private, online and gun show sales.
2. Reinstate an updated assault weapons ban covering high-capacity magazines, with no sunset clause.
3. Appropriate sustained funding for CDC and NIH gun violence research.
4. Fund implementation of state extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia.

Definitions, age ranges and methodology notes are in the data appendix. Contact: Northgate Progress Institute, Office of Publications.

# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET

Media contact: Northgate Progress Institute, Office of Publications, [email], [phone]

# New NPI brief: Close the background-check gap, reinstate the assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, publishes Oct. 27

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens. A brief published today by the Northgate Progress Institute shows two gaps in federal law help keep that toll running, and that Congress can close both.

In "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention Dr. Jamal Whitfield documents a background-check system with a hole in its center: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years before a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and half of private sales involved no check at all.

The second gap is measured in mass casualties: mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban than outside it, in an analysis of 1981-2017 data, and states with high-capacity magazine bans have 48% fewer mass shooting incidents.

"The numbers are not ambiguous," Whitfield said. "One in five recent gun acquisitions involved no background check at all. The deadliest rifles went back on the market the day the ban expired. Closing these gaps is not radical. It is the least Congress owes the 46,728 Americans we lost in a single year."

The brief asks Congress to require background checks on every firearm sale and transfer; reinstate an updated, permanent assault weapons ban covering high-capacity magazines; fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH; and fund state extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia.

The brief and data appendix are at [URL]. Embargoed copies: [email].

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens (CDC, 2023).
- Two gaps in federal law help make that toll possible: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years before a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and no federal assault weapons ban has been in force since the 1994 law expired in 2004.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate an updated assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help the states that have not yet adopted extreme-risk laws do so.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, gunfire killed 46,728 people in the United States, the third-highest annual total ever recorded (CDC). Averaged across a year, that is one death every 11 minutes: a father on his commute, a grandmother alone at home, a teenager at a bus stop.

Two stories sit inside that number, and only one of them is improving. Gun homicides have fallen from their pandemic peak, from 20,958 in 2021 to 17,927 in 2023, but that remains the fifth-highest total on record. Gun suicides keep climbing: 27,300 people died by gun suicide in 2023, a record for the third consecutive year, and suicides have accounted for the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995 (CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions).

Neither number is weather. Both track a decision the country has made about how easily people in crisis or conflict can obtain a firearm, and it is a decision Congress can change.

### 2. Children and teens

The toll is steepest among the young. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, killing more of them in 2023 than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer, and they have held that ranking for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In all, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire in 2023, an average of seven every day. Measured more broadly, among all Americans ages 1 to 19, the firearm death rate is 5.9 per 100,000, ranging from 1.2 per 100,000 in Massachusetts to 16.1 in Louisiana (America's Health Rankings, pooled 2021-2023). The distance between those two numbers is not luck. It is policy.

Most of those deaths were homicides, and nearly a third were suicides. It is a ranking young Americans did not hold before 2020, and it is not a ranking a wealthy country should accept.

### 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed dealer sells a firearm. Since 1994, that has been nearly the whole of the federal requirement. Transfers between individuals, sales arranged online and purchases at gun shows are governed by a patchwork of state laws, and in most states no check is required at all. A stranger at a kitchen table, a listing on a phone screen, a folding table at a weekend gun show: in much of the country, a prohibited purchaser can choose any of the three and buy a gun with no questions asked.

The hole in the middle of that system is measurable. In a 2015 national survey, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a gun in the previous two years said they did so without a background check. Among private purchases, guns bought somewhere other than a store or pawnshop, the share acquired with no check at all was 50% (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Background checks are not a formality. Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, the system has screened more than 314 million applications and denied an estimated 4.8 million of them (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2023). Each denial is a purchase attempt the law has stopped.

And states that close the gap see results. When Connecticut began requiring a background check on every handgun purchase in 1995, the state's firearm suicide rate fell by an estimated 15% in the years that followed (Crifasi et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015). Connecticut paired its check with a purchaser permit; the principle is the same for any state that closes its private-sale loophole, and for a Congress that closes it nationally.

Voters are not divided on this. In a 2023 national poll, 86% of American adults said Congress should require background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, including 80% of Republicans (McCourtney Institute for Democracy, 2023).

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, an average of nearly two a day, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 were injured. It was the second-highest yearly total in the archive's records. Semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines have become a signature of the deadliest of these attacks: the shooters in Parkland (2018), Uvalde (2022) and Lewiston (2023) each used one, and the Uvalde killer carried seven 30-round magazines.

Rifles of all kinds are used in only about 2% to 3% of U.S. murders (FBI, 2017-2018), but volume is the wrong measure here; the case against assault weapons is a case about lethality in the minutes before anyone can intervene.

The country has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law banned the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data spanning 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban years (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). A multivariate study of state laws covering 1984 to 2017 found that states with bans on high-capacity magazines had 48% fewer mass shooting incidents (Webster et al., 2020). The decade-level comparison runs in the same direction: high-fatality mass shooting deaths fell 43% from the 10 years before the ban to the 10 years it was in force, then rose 239% in the decade after it lapsed (Klarevas, Rampage Nation, 2016).

On Sept. 13, 2004, the ban did not fail. It expired, under a sunset clause Congress wrote into the original law, and the weapons it had taken off the civilian market came back. Restoring that law, updated to cover the rifles marketed since 2004 and made permanent, is the clearest single step Congress can take against mass-casualty violence. Extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia, are the third tool: they allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others, and they work best when the federal gaps above them are closed.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and gun show purchases, and apply the same record-keeping requirements and penalties that govern licensed dealers.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban on the manufacture, sale and transfer of assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that feed them, write it to cover the detachable-magazine rifles marketed since 2004, and make it permanent, with no sunset clause.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, so prevention policy is built on data rather than left to drift with each appropriations cycle.
4. **Incentivize extreme-risk laws.** Fund implementation of extreme-risk protection order laws in the 22 states and the District of Columbia that have enacted them, and create grant incentives for states that have not.

Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not an inevitability. It is the measurable result of gaps Congress chose to leave open, and gaps Congress has the power to close.

# Data appendix: Safer Communities Brief No. 9

**Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026 | Draft for editorial review

This appendix carries every figure used in the brief, the fact sheet, the press release and the social cards. Per the NPI style sheet (rev. 3), definitions, denominators, population bases and methodology notes appear here rather than in body copy (B1-B6), and each source line follows format C1. Figures marked with a dagger (†) were added at production stage from the cited sources; all others come from the compiled source tables.

---

## A1. National gun deaths, 2023, with trend

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Total gun deaths, 2023 | 46,728 (third-highest annual total on record) |
| Gun suicide deaths, 2023 | 27,300 (58% of all gun deaths; record high for the third consecutive year) |
| Gun homicide deaths | 20,958 (2021); 19,651 (2022); 17,927 (2023) |
| Gun homicide ranking, 2023 | Fifth-highest total on record; down nearly 9% from 2022 |
| Suicides as a share of gun deaths | Majority every year since 1995 |
| Frequency | One gun death every 11 minutes |

Source: CDC, National Vital Statistics System, WONDER Multiple Cause of Death, 2023, https://wonder.cdc.gov/ ; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic," June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data-2023

Notes: Final 2023 mortality data. Rankings ("third-highest," "fifth-highest") and the 11-minute frequency are Johns Hopkins analyses of CDC data. Per style sheet B2, the intent breakdown appears here, not in body copy. The overall gun death rate fell 3.4% from 2022 to 2023 (about 1,476 fewer deaths).

## A2. Gun deaths among children and teens, ages 1-17, 2023

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Total gun deaths | 2,566 |
| Death rate | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Leading cause of death | Firearms, for the fourth consecutive year (since 2020) |
| Compared with other causes | More deaths than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer |
| Average per day | 7 (2,566 divided by 365) |
| Intent | Homicide 63%; suicide 29%; unintentional 5%; undetermined/other 3% |

Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Annual Gun Violence Data 2023" (analysis of CDC WONDER), June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data-2023 ; The Trace, "American Gun Deaths Declined in 2023 — Except Among Children," August 2024, https://www.thetrace.org/2024/08/gun-deaths-cdc-data-homicide-suicide/

Notes: Age range is 1 through 17, the population in the Johns Hopkins leading-cause analysis; infants under 1 are excluded, as is standard for cause-of-death ranking. Johns Hopkins authors note that for some single-year age groups within 1-17, guns are among the leading causes of death but not the top cause; the "fourth consecutive year" ranking is for the 1-17 group as a whole. Intent shares are rounded and sum to more than 100% because of rounding.

## A3. Firearm death rate, youth ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| U.S. rate, any intent | 5.9 per 100,000 |
| Lowest state | Massachusetts, 1.2 per 100,000 |
| Highest state | Louisiana, 16.1 per 100,000 |

Source: America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Explore Firearm Deaths, Children," 2021-2023, https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/firearm_deaths_children

Notes: † Ages 1-19 include 18- and 19-year-olds, unlike A2; all intents (unintentional, suicide, homicide, undetermined). Three-year pooled CDC WONDER data. The state contrast in brief copy is descriptive; the appendix does not attribute the state gap to any single policy.

## A4. Gun acquisitions without background checks, 2015 survey

| Measure | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Acquisitions without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16-27) |
| Private purchases without a background check | 50% (95% CI, 35-65) |

Source: Miller M., Hepburn L., Azrael D., "Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey," Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590

Notes: 2015 nationally representative survey of 1,613 gun owners reporting on their most recent firearm acquisition within the previous two years; self-reported; "private purchases" are those from someone other than a store or pawnshop, including between individuals, online and at gun shows. Some acquisitions made without a check may have been lawful in the owner's state (for example, certain gifts and inheritances). The widely quoted ~40% figure from the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook and Ludwig) measured recent acquisitions that did not go through a licensed dealer, including gifts and inheritances, and was not a direct question about background checks; re-analysis limited to sales put the comparable figure far lower (14-22%). House style (rev. 3, B4) uses the Miller et al. estimate.

## A5. Background checks performed and denied since the Brady Act

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Applications subject to background checks, 1994-2021 | More than 314 million |
| Applications denied | Nearly 4.8 million |
| Denial rate | About 1.5% |

Source: Bureau of Justice Statistics, "Background Checks for Firearm Transfers, 2021," May 2023, https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/bcft21.pdf

Notes: † Estimated totals since the Brady Act's effective date, FBI and state checking agencies combined. Not every denial reflects a prohibited purchaser; some denials are later overturned on appeal. Denials should not be read as counts of prevented crimes.

## A6. Connecticut permit-to-purchase law and firearm suicide

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Firearm suicide rate after Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law | Estimated 15.4% reduction |

Source: Crifasi C.K., Meyers J.S., Vernick J.S., Webster D.W., "Effects of changes in permit-to-purchase handgun laws in Connecticut and Missouri on suicide rates," Preventive Medicine, October 2015, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ypmed.2015.07.013

Notes: † Quasi-experimental synthetic control analysis of state-level suicide data, 1981-2012. Brief copy rounds 15.4% to 15%. Connecticut's law pairs the background check with a purchaser permit, so the estimate applies to the combined policy, not to a check alone. The same study associates Missouri's 2007 repeal of its permit law with an increase in firearm suicide rates.

## A7. Public support for universal background checks

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers | 86% of American adults |
| Republican support | 80% |

Source: McCourtney Institute for Democracy (Penn State), Mood of the Nation Poll, fielded May 12-18, 2023, https://www.mprnews.org/story/2023/07/25/poll-majority--support-universal-background-checks-gun-licensing-assault-weapons-ban

Notes: † National adult sample; question asks about a congressional mandate for all sales and transfers, including private, online and gun show sales. Most recent general-population figure verified at production time; substitute a newer NPI poll if one is fielded before copy deadline.

## A8. Mass shootings, 2023 (Gun Violence Archive)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass shootings | 656 |
| People killed | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |
| Average per day | 1.8 (656 divided by 365) |
| Ranking | Second-highest yearly total in GVA records; highest was 689 in 2021 |

Source: Gun Violence Archive, "Mass Shootings in 2023," 2024, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/reports/mass-shooting?year=2023 ; Axios, "Mass shootings increased in 2023. But gun deaths went down," January 9, 2024, https://www.axios.com/2024/01/09/mass-shooting-gun-violence-us-2023 ; The Trace, "Gun Violence by the Numbers in 2023," December 2023, https://www.thetrace.org/2023/12/data-gun-violence-deaths-america/

Notes: GVA defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, in a single event at the same general time and location, not including the shooter (style sheet B5). GVA counts are subject to revision as incidents are re-verified. Databases with different definitions produce different counts of different quantities: the AP/USA Today/Northeastern University Mass Killing Database (four or more killed, not including the perpetrator, within 24 hours, any weapon; https://apnews.com/projects/mass-shooting-killings-united-states/) counted 29 mass killings in 2023. The compiled source table's entry of 36 mass killings in 2023 "as of late October" is a partial-year figure and does not match that database's full-year count; it is not used in copy and should be re-checked before any future use.

## A9. Assault-style rifles used in three recent mass shootings

| Incident | Date | Rifle | Killed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Fla. | Feb. 14, 2018 | Smith & Wesson M&P15 Sport II | 17 |
| Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, Texas | May 24, 2022 | Daniel Defense DDM4 V7; seven 30-round magazines | 21 (19 students, 2 teachers) |
| Lewiston, Maine | Oct. 25, 2023 | Ruger SFAR .308; 25-round magazines | 18 |

Source: Violence Policy Center, "Large Capacity Ammunition Magazines," https://www.vpc.org/fact_sht/VPCshootinglist.pdf ; Maine State Police, "After-Action Assessment of the October 25, 2023 Lewiston Mass Shooting," 2024, https://www.maine.gov/dps/msp/sites/maine.gov.dps.msp/files/inline-files/AAR.pdf ; NPR, "What to know about the AR-15, the gun used in the Uvalde shooting," May 26, 2022, https://www.npr.org/2022/05/26/1101274322/uvalde-ar-15-style-rifle-history-shooter-mass-shooting

Notes: † Casualty counts are public record and exclude the perpetrators, each of whom died during or after the attack. NPI copy names no victims. "Assault weapons" follows the category defined in the author's outline (semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines addressed by the 1994-2004 federal ban and its successors); the FBI does not separately track AR-style rifles (see A10).

## A10. Rifles in U.S. murders, 2017-2018 (FBI)

| Measure | 2017 | 2018 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rifle murders (all types) | 390 | 297 |
| All murders in FBI SHR data | 15,195 | 14,123 |
| Murders in which the weapon was identified | n/a | 10,093 |
| Rifle share | 2.6% of all murders | 2.1% of all murders; 2.9% of murders with a known weapon |

Source: FBI, Crime in the United States 2018, Expanded Homicide Data Tables 8 and 11, 2019, https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2018/crime-in-the-u.s.-2018/tables/expanded-homicide-data-table-8.xls

Notes: The FBI does not distinguish AR-style or other semiautomatic rifles from hunting rifles, and weapon-type breakdowns are not comparable after the FBI's transition to NIBRS. The compiled source table cited "2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018)"; recomputed from FBI counts, the 2018 share is 2.1% of all murders or 2.9% of murders in which police identified the weapon. Brief copy therefore says "about 2% to 3%." Presented per style sheet B6 (one sentence in body copy, then mass-casualty lethality).

## A11. The federal ban period and mass-shooting fatality rates

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass-shooting fatalities during the 1994-2004 ban period | 70% less likely to occur (relative rate 0.30; 95% CI, 0.22-0.39) |

Source: DiMaggio C., Avraham J., Berry C., Bukur M., Feldman J., Klein M., Shah N., Tandon M., Frangos S., "Changes in US mass shooting deaths associated with the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban: Analysis of open-source data," Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30188421/

Notes: Analysis of open-source, media-verified mass-shooting data spanning 1981-2017; compares the ban period with non-ban years, controlling for yearly trend, using regression on fatality rates per firearm homicide and per U.S. population. The ban (Public Law 103-159, effective September 13, 1994) covered a defined set of semiautomatic rifles, pistols and shotguns and magazines holding more than 10 rounds, and carried the 10-year sunset that took effect September 13, 2004. This is an observational before-after design; the association is not proof of causation.

## A12. State high-capacity magazine bans and mass shootings

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass shooting incidents in states with high-capacity magazine bans | 48% reduction (statistically significant) |
| Mass shooting fatalities in the same models | 33% reduction (suggestive; not statistically significant) |

Source: Webster et al. (2020), as assessed in RAND Corporation, Gun Policy in America, "Effects of Assault Weapon and High-Capacity Magazine Bans on Mass Shootings," updated January 29, 2026, https://www.rand.org/research/gun-policy/analysis/ban-assault-weapons/mass-shootings.html

Notes: Negative binomial models of state panel data, 1984-2017; mass shootings defined as four or more killed, excluding the shooter, with drug- and gang-motivated incidents excluded; controlling for 14 firearm laws, state fixed effects, linear and quadratic time trends, and 14 social and economic covariates. The same study found uncertain evidence for assault weapons bans specifically; RAND's overall rating is that high-capacity magazine bans "may decrease mass shootings; evidence limited," and that evidence on assault weapons bans and mass shootings is inconclusive.

## A13. The ban decade versus the decades on either side

| Comparison | Change |
| --- | --- |
| High-fatality mass shooting incidents, decade before the ban → ban decade | Down 37% |
| High-fatality mass shooting deaths, decade before the ban → ban decade | Down 43% |
| Mass shootings, ban decade → decade after expiration | Up 183% |
| Deaths, ban decade → decade after expiration | Up 239% |

Source: Klarevas L., "Rampage Nation: Securing America from Mass Shootings," 2016, via Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, "Research Supports Tighter Gun Laws to Reduce Mass Shooting Violence," https://www.publichealth.columbia.edu/news/research-supports-tighter-gun-laws-reduce-mass-shooting-violence

Notes: † Ten-year before-and-after comparison of the federal ban period (September 1994 to September 2004); "high-fatality mass shootings" refers in Klarevas's analysis to incidents with six or more people killed. Simple before-after comparisons cannot separate the ban from other period effects and are presented as descriptive corroboration, not causal proof.

## A14. State extreme-risk (ERPO) laws

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| States with ERPO laws in force | 22 states, plus the District of Columbia and the U.S. Virgin Islands |

Source: National ERPO Resource Center, "State-by-State," February 2026, https://erpo.org/state-by-state/

Notes: † ERPO laws authorize civil court orders that temporarily prohibit firearm purchase and possession by individuals found to pose a danger to themselves or others. Count current as of February 2026.

---

**General notes.** (1) Figures without a dagger come from the compiled source tables dated October 8, 2026; daggers mark figures added at production stage from the cited sources, all verified against primary or closely secondary documentation. (2) Studies of the 1994-2004 ban and of state bans are observational; no randomized evidence exists, and independent systematic reviews (RAND, Gun Policy in America, updated January 2026) rate the evidence base as limited to inconclusive. NPI cites these studies for what they show, with that limitation stated. (3) All copy in this package is draft; publication is subject to approval by the Director of Publications.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Fact sheet for congressional offices

## Closing the gaps: universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026
Author: Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention | Full data appendix available with the brief

**THE TOLL**

**1. 46,728 gun deaths in 2023; one every 11 minutes.** The third-highest annual total on record.
Source: CDC WONDER, 2023, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**2. 58% were suicides: 27,300 people, a record for the third straight year.** Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995. Gun homicides, 17,927 in 2023, fell from 20,958 in 2021 but remain the fifth-highest total on record.
Source: CDC WONDER, 2023, via Johns Hopkins CGVS, June 2025.

**3. Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, for the fourth consecutive year.** 2,566 died by gunfire in 2023, an average of seven a day, more than car crashes, overdoses or cancer.
Source: Johns Hopkins analysis of CDC data, 2023.

**THE GAPS**

**4. 22% of recent gun acquisitions involved no background check.** Among private purchases (not from a store or pawnshop), half involved no check.
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**5. The check system screens and stops.** More than 314 million applications screened since the Brady Act took effect in 1994; nearly 4.8 million denied.
Source: Bureau of Justice Statistics, May 2023.

**6. 656 mass shootings in 2023: 712 killed, 2,692 injured.** The second-highest yearly total on record.
Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023.

**THE EVIDENCE**

**7. Mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban**, in an analysis of mass-shooting data spanning 1981-2017.
Source: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019.

**8. States with bans on high-capacity magazines had 48% fewer mass shooting incidents**, in an analysis of state laws spanning 1984-2017.
Source: Webster et al., 2020, as assessed in RAND Gun Policy in America, 2026.

**PUBLIC SUPPORT**

86% of American adults, including 80% of Republicans, support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers.
Source: McCourtney Institute for Democracy, Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023.

**WHAT THE BRIEF ASKS OF CONGRESS**

1. Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private, online and gun show sales.
2. Reinstate an updated assault weapons ban covering high-capacity magazines, with no sunset clause.
3. Appropriate sustained funding for CDC and NIH gun violence research.
4. Fund implementation of state extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia.

Definitions, age ranges and methodology notes are in the data appendix. Contact: Northgate Progress Institute, Office of Publications.

# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET

Media contact: Northgate Progress Institute, Office of Publications, [email], [phone]

# New NPI brief: Close the background-check gap, reinstate the assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, publishes Oct. 27

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens. A brief published today by the Northgate Progress Institute shows two gaps in federal law help keep that toll running, and that Congress can close both.

In "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention Dr. Jamal Whitfield documents a background-check system with a hole in its center: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the two years before a 2015 national survey did so without a background check, and half of private sales involved no check at all.

The second gap is measured in mass casualties: mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban than outside it, in an analysis of 1981-2017 data, and states with high-capacity magazine bans have 48% fewer mass shooting incidents.

"The numbers are not ambiguous," Whitfield said. "One in five recent gun acquisitions involved no background check at all. The deadliest rifles went back on the market the day the ban expired. Closing these gaps is not radical. It is the least Congress owes the 46,728 Americans we lost in a single year."

The brief asks Congress to require background checks on every firearm sale and transfer; reinstate an updated, permanent assault weapons ban covering high-capacity magazines; fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH; and fund state extreme-risk laws, now enacted in 22 states and the District of Columbia.

The brief and data appendix are at [URL]. Embargoed copies: [email].
